title: Design a chart audit
brief: Your district hospital wants to audit compliance with the hand hygiene (HH) policy. The aim is to estimate the current compliance rate across all wards. There are 8 wards, each with 4–6 clinical staff per shift. Audits must be done by a trained observer. You have one trained observer available for 2 hours per week.

task.stem: Which audit design best fits this aim and these constraints?

options.label: Systematic random sample: observe every 3rd opportunity across all wards during the 2 hours each week; rotate start ward weekly to avoid bias.
Observe all hand hygiene opportunities in Ward 1 only for the full 2 hours each week, then report a hospital-wide rate.
Ask each ward in-charge to self-report their ward's compliance rate at the end of the month.
Observe all 8 wards simultaneously by dividing 15 minutes per ward.

debrief.correct: Yes. A systematic random sample spread across all wards — with ward rotation — gives you a defensible hospital-wide estimate within your resource constraint. It avoids the two main biases: convenience bias (always observing the most accessible ward) and Hawthorne effect clustering (staff in one ward learn they are being watched and change behaviour, inflating the rate).
debrief.wrong: Observing only one ward gives a ward rate, not a hospital-wide rate — it cannot be generalised. Self-reporting by ward in-charges is not an audit; it is self-assessment, which consistently overestimates compliance because of social-desirability bias. Splitting 15 minutes across 8 wards simultaneously requires 8 observers — you have one. The only feasible design that covers the whole hospital is a systematic sample with rotation, even if each week's sample is small.
debrief.rule_cited: Audit sampling design — NAHQ HQ Essentials; IHI QI 102 measurement planning.
